before: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6(b), a consumer who reports a lost or stolen debit card within two business days of learning of it owes at most the lesser of $50 or the transfers made before notice; after two business days the cap rises to $500. Transfers shown on a periodic statement that aren't reported within 60 days of the statement being sent carry unlimited liability for transfers after that 60-day window. The 2- and 60-day clocks run from different starts: learning of the loss, and the statement's transmittal.
after: If you report a lost or stolen debit card within two business days of finding out, you pay at most $50 of what was taken before you told the bank. After two business days, the most you pay rises to $500. And if a payment you didn’t make is on a statement and you don’t report it within 60 days of the statement being sent, you can be made to pay all of what’s taken after those 60 days. The two days start when you find out; the 60 days start when the statement is sent. This is Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6(b), under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act.

before: Truth in Lending Act, Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.12(b)(1)(ii): a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card use is capped at the lesser of $50 or the amount obtained before the card issuer is notified.
after: If someone uses your credit card without your permission, you pay at most $50, or less if less was spent before you told the card’s issuer. This is the Truth in Lending Act’s Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.12(b)(1)(ii).

before: Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.11: the bank must decide within 10 business days (20 for a new account's first 30 days); if it takes longer it must provisionally credit the account within 10 business days and may take up to 45 days, or 90 days for point-of-sale debit card, out-of-state or new-account transfers. Results go to the consumer within 3 business days of finishing.
after: The bank has 10 business days to decide, or 20 for a payment in a new account’s first 30 days. If it needs longer, it must put the money back in your account for now within those 10 business days, and it can then take up to 45 days, or 90 for a debit card purchase, a payment made from outside the US or one on a new account. It tells you the result within 3 business days of deciding. This is Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.11.

before: Debit cards fall under the voluntary Canadian Code of Practice for Consumer Debit Card Services (section 5): the cardholder isn't liable for losses from circumstances beyond their control, including being the victim of fraud, theft or coercion, technical failures, and use after the card is reported lost or stolen. A cardholder who contributed (for example by voluntarily sharing a PIN or not reporting in reasonable time) can be liable, but no more than the card's withdrawal limits, and more only where overdraft or a linked credit line is attached. There’s no statutory dollar cap for debit.
after: You don’t pay for losses you couldn’t control: fraud, theft or being forced to use the card, a technical failure, or use after you reported the card lost or stolen. If you contributed to the loss, say by choosing to share your PIN or by not reporting it in reasonable time, you can be made to pay, but no more than the card’s withdrawal limits, unless an overdraft or a linked credit line is attached. No law sets a dollar limit for debit cards: this is the voluntary Canadian Code of Practice for Consumer Debit Card Services, section 5.

before: Bank Act, S.C. 1991, c. 46, s. 627.33: a borrower's maximum liability for unauthorized use of a credit card issued in Canada is $50 unless they showed gross negligence (gross fault in Quebec), and nothing after they report the card lost, stolen or at risk. Use of the PIN alone doesn't prove gross negligence. For non-bank federally regulated issuers, FCAC says the cap is the lesser of $50 or the agreement's amount.
after: If someone uses your credit card without your permission, you pay at most C$50, unless you were grossly negligent (gross fault, in Quebec), and nothing after you report the card lost, stolen or at risk. A payment made with your PIN doesn’t prove gross negligence on its own. For card issuers that aren’t banks but are federally regulated, the FCAC says the limit is C$50 or the amount in your agreement, whichever is less. This is the Bank Act, S.C. 1991, c. 46, s. 627.33.

before: Debit Card Code of Practice: the issuer must respond to a report of an unauthorized transaction as soon as possible and in no more than 10 business days, a limit it can pause while waiting for a signed statement or affidavit. No statutory refund deadline is set for credit cards.
after: Under the Debit Card Code of Practice, the bank must answer your report of a payment you didn’t make as soon as it can, within 10 business days, though it can stop that clock while it waits for a signed statement or affidavit from you. No law sets a deadline to refund a credit card payment.

before: Banco de México's card rules, in force since 2019 as CONDUSEF describes them, require a bank told of unrecognized charges to credit the account by the second banking business day for transactions made in the 48 hours before the report. Older charges go through the general dispute (aclaración) process of Article 23 of the Ley para la Transparencia y Ordenamiento de los Servicios Financieros, which sets no peso cap on the customer's loss.
after: Report charges you don’t recognize, and the bank must put back any made in the 48 hours before your report by the second banking business day. Older charges go through the general dispute process (aclaración) under Article 23 of the Ley para la Transparencia y Ordenamiento de los Servicios Financieros, which sets no limit in pesos on what you can lose. These are Banco de México’s card rules, in force since 2019, as CONDUSEF describes them.

before: No statutory peso cap found. The same Banco de México rules (48-hour window, credit by the second business day) apply to credit cards, and under Article 23 of the Ley para la Transparencia y Ordenamiento de los Servicios Financieros a cardholder may withhold payment of a disputed charge, without interest or late fees and without being reported to a credit bureau, until the claim is resolved.
after: No law was found that limits what you pay, in pesos. The same Banco de México rules apply to credit cards: charges from the 48 hours before your report are put back by the second business day. Under Article 23 of the Ley para la Transparencia y Ordenamiento de los Servicios Financieros, you can hold back payment of a disputed charge until your claim is settled, with no interest or late fee and without being reported to a credit bureau.

before: Charges from the 48 hours before the report are credited by the second banking business day (Banco de México rules, per CONDUSEF). Under Article 23 LTOSF the institution must answer a dispute within 45 days, or 180 days for foreign transactions; CONDUSEF says an unanswered claim is treated as resolved in the customer's favor.
after: Charges from the 48 hours before your report come back by the second banking business day (Banco de México’s rules, as CONDUSEF describes them). For other disputes, the bank must answer within 45 days, or 180 for a payment abroad, under Article 23 of the LTOSF. CONDUSEF says a claim left unanswered is settled in your favor.

before: Payment Services Regulations 2017, reg. 77: the payer can be made to bear up to £35 of losses from a lost, stolen or misappropriated payment instrument, but nothing if the loss wasn't detectable before the payment, was caused by the provider's staff or agents, happened after notification, or strong customer authentication was required and not applied. A payer who acted fraudulently or failed their obligations with intent or gross negligence bears all the losses.
after: You can be made to pay up to £35 of what’s lost on a lost, stolen or misused card, and nothing if you couldn’t have noticed the loss before the payment, if the bank’s staff or agents caused it, if it happened after you told the bank, or if the bank didn’t apply strong customer authentication (a second check, such as a code sent to your phone) where it was required. If you acted fraudulently, or broke your obligations on purpose or through gross negligence, you pay all of it. This is the Payment Services Regulations 2017, reg. 77.

before: Consumer Credit Act 1974, s. 84(1): a debtor under a credit-token (credit card) agreement can be made liable for misuse only up to £35, or the credit limit if lower, and s. 84(3) ends even that once the issuer has been told the card is lost or stolen. The PSRs 2017 reg. 77 cap of £35 also applies to cards as payment instruments.
after: If your credit card is misused, you can be made to pay at most £35, or your credit limit if that’s lower, and nothing once you’ve told the card’s issuer it’s lost or stolen (Consumer Credit Act 1974, s. 84(1) and (3)). The same £35 limit in the Payment Services Regulations 2017, reg. 77, covers cards too.

before: PSRs 2017, reg. 76: the provider must refund as soon as practicable and no later than the end of the business day after it becomes aware of the unauthorized transaction, unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect the customer of fraud and notifies the authorities under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.
after: Your bank must refund you as soon as it can, and by the end of the next business day after it learns of the payment, unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect you of fraud and reports it to the authorities under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. This is the Payment Services Regulations 2017, reg. 76.

before: European Union (Payment Services) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 6 of 2018), reg. 98, transposing PSD2 Art. 74: the payer bears up to €50 of losses from a lost, stolen or misappropriated payment instrument, but nothing if the loss wasn't detectable before the payment, was caused by the provider's staff or agents, or strong customer authentication wasn't required. Fraud, or intentional or grossly negligent breach of the payer's obligations under reg. 93, removes the cap.
after: You pay up to €50 of what’s lost on a lost, stolen or misused card, and nothing if you couldn’t have noticed the loss before the payment, if the bank’s staff or agents caused it, or if the bank didn’t ask for strong customer authentication (a second check, such as a code sent to your phone). If you acted fraudulently, or broke your obligations under reg. 93 on purpose or through gross negligence, there’s no limit. This is the European Union (Payment Services) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 6 of 2018), reg. 98, which brings in Article 74 of the EU’s PSD2.

before: The same S.I. 6/2018 reg. 98 €50 cap covers credit cards, as they are payment instruments under PSD2.
after: The same €50 limit covers credit cards, since they’re payment instruments under PSD2 (S.I. 6/2018, reg. 98).

before: S.I. 6/2018, reg. 97(1): refund immediately and no later than the end of the business day after the provider notes or is notified of the transaction, unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud and communicates them to the Central Bank.
after: Your bank must refund you at once, and by the end of the next business day after it notices the payment or is told of it, unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud and gives them to the Central Bank (S.I. 6/2018, reg. 97(1)).

before: Lög um greiðsluþjónustu nr. 114/2021 (Payment Services Act), art. 80, Iceland's PSD2 transposition: the payer bears losses up to the equivalent of €50 in krónur, at the official mid-rate, from a lost, stolen or misused payment instrument, but nothing if they couldn't have noticed the loss, the provider's staff caused it, it happened after notice, or strong customer authentication wasn't required. Fraud, or intentional or grossly negligent breach of the art. 75 duties, removes the cap.
after: You pay up to the value of €50 in krónur, at the official mid-rate, of what’s lost on a lost, stolen or misused card, and nothing if you couldn’t have noticed the loss, the bank’s staff caused it, it happened after you told the bank, or the bank didn’t ask for strong customer authentication (a second check, such as a code sent to your phone). If you acted fraudulently, or broke your duties under art. 75 on purpose or through gross negligence, there’s no limit. This is Iceland’s Payment Services Act, Lög um greiðsluþjónustu nr. 114/2021, art. 80, which brings in PSD2.

before: Art. 80 of Act 114/2021 applies to any payment instrument, credit cards included: up to the ISK equivalent of €50.
after: The same limit, the value of €50 in krónur, covers credit cards too: art. 80 of Act 114/2021 applies to any payment instrument.

before: Act 114/2021, art. 79: refund at once and no later than the end of the next business day after discovery or notice; a provider suspecting fraud may refuse and must report it to the Financial Supervisory Authority.
after: Your bank must refund you at once, and by the end of the next business day after it finds out or is told. A bank that suspects fraud may refuse, and must report it to the Financial Supervisory Authority (Act 114/2021, art. 79).

before: Code monétaire et financier, art. L133-19: before notice, the payer bears losses from a lost or stolen instrument up to €50, but nothing if the transaction was made without the personalized security data, the loss wasn't detectable, the provider's staff caused it, the card was used remotely without the payer's knowledge, it was counterfeited while in their possession, or strong authentication wasn't required. Fraud, or intentional or grossly negligent breach of arts. L133-16 and L133-17, makes the payer bear all losses.
after: Until you tell the bank, you pay up to €50 of what’s lost on a lost or stolen card, and nothing if the payment was made without your PIN or other security details, you couldn’t have noticed the loss, the bank’s staff caused it, the card was used remotely without your knowledge, it was copied while you still had it, or the bank didn’t ask for strong authentication. If you acted fraudulently, or broke your obligations under articles L133-16 and L133-17 on purpose or through gross negligence, you pay all of it. This is the Code monétaire et financier, art. L133-19.

before: Art. L133-19 CMF covers every payment instrument, credit cards included: €50 cap on the same terms.
after: The same €50 limit, on the same terms, covers credit cards: art. L133-19 of the Code monétaire et financier applies to every payment instrument.

before: Code monétaire et financier, art. L133-18: refund at the latest by the end of the first business day after the provider learns of the unauthorized transaction.
after: Your bank must refund you by the end of the first business day after it learns of the payment (Code monétaire et financier, art. L133-18).

before: Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch (BGB) §675v: the payment provider can claim up to €50 for losses from a lost, stolen or misused payment instrument, but nothing if the payer couldn't have noticed the loss, the provider's staff caused it, or the provider didn't require strong customer authentication. Fraudulent intent, or intentional or grossly negligent breach of §675l duties, makes the payer liable for the whole loss.
after: Your bank can make you pay up to €50 of what’s lost on a lost, stolen or misused card, and nothing if you couldn’t have noticed the loss, the bank’s staff caused it, or the bank didn’t ask for strong customer authentication (a second check, such as a code sent to your phone). If you acted fraudulently, or broke your duties under §675l on purpose or through gross negligence, you pay all of it. This is the Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch (BGB), §675v.

before: BGB §675v applies to every payment instrument (Zahlungsinstrument), credit cards included: €50 on the same terms.
after: The same €50 limit, on the same terms, covers credit cards: BGB §675v applies to every payment instrument (Zahlungsinstrument).

before: BGB §675u: refund without delay, at the latest by the end of the business day after the day the provider was told of or learned about the unauthorized transaction.
after: Your bank must refund you without delay, and by the end of the business day after it’s told of the payment or learns of it (BGB §675u).

before: Real Decreto-ley 19/2018, art. 46: the payer can be made to bear up to €50 of losses from a lost, stolen or misappropriated instrument, but nothing if the loss wasn't detectable or the provider's staff caused it, and nothing for card-not-present use of only the data printed on the card, for use after notice, or where strong customer authentication wasn't required. Fraud, or intentional or grossly negligent breach of art. 41 duties, removes the cap.
after: You can be made to pay up to €50 of what’s lost on a lost, stolen or misused card, and nothing if you couldn’t have noticed the loss or the bank’s staff caused it. You also pay nothing for online or phone payments made with only the details printed on the card, for anything after you told the bank, or where the bank didn’t ask for strong customer authentication (a second check, such as a code sent to your phone). If you acted fraudulently, or broke your duties under art. 41 on purpose or through gross negligence, there’s no limit. This is Real Decreto-ley 19/2018, art. 46.

before: RDL 19/2018 art. 46 covers every payment instrument, credit cards included: €50 on the same terms.
after: The same €50 limit, on the same terms, covers credit cards: art. 46 of RDL 19/2018 applies to every payment instrument.

before: RDL 19/2018, art. 45: refund immediately and at the latest by the end of the business day after the transaction is noticed or notified, unless the provider has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud and tells the Bank of Spain in writing.
after: Your bank must refund you at once, and by the end of the business day after it notices the payment or is told of it, unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud and tells the Bank of Spain in writing (RDL 19/2018, art. 45).

before: No law caps debit card purchase losses. The Depositor Protection Act (Act No. 94 of 2005) covers only ATM withdrawals with forged or stolen cash cards: forged-card withdrawals are void unless the depositor acted intentionally or with gross negligence (art. 4); for a stolen card the bank must repay withdrawals made from 30 days before the depositor's prompt notice (art. 5), in full, or three quarters if the bank proves ordinary negligence, and nothing for gross negligence or theft by a family member. Earlier withdrawals aren’t covered.
after: No law limits what you lose on debit card purchases. The Depositor Protection Act (Act No. 94 of 2005) covers only cash machine withdrawals with a forged or stolen cash card. A withdrawal with a forged card is treated as never made, unless you acted on purpose or with gross negligence (art. 4). For a stolen card, the bank must repay withdrawals made from 30 days before you promptly reported it (art. 5): in full, or three quarters if the bank proves you were negligent, and nothing if you were grossly negligent or a family member took it. Withdrawals before those 30 days aren’t covered.

before: No statutory cap on credit card liability was found for Japan; protection for unauthorized credit card use is set by each issuer's card member terms, not by law.
after: No law was found that limits what you pay when your credit card is misused in Japan: each card issuer’s member terms set the protection, not the law.

before: Electronic Financial Transactions Act art. 9: the bank must pay losses from forged or altered access media, errors in processing, and access media obtained by hacking into networks, unless the user acted intentionally or with gross negligence under a prior written agreement; art. 10 covers loss and theft of access media. The Specialized Credit Financial Business Act art. 16(1) makes the issuer liable for debit card use from the moment it’s told the card is lost or stolen. No statutory cap on a debit cardholder's loss before notice was found.
after: Your bank must pay for losses from a forged or altered card or login, a processing error, or details stolen by hacking, unless you acted on purpose or with gross negligence under a written agreement made beforehand (Electronic Financial Transactions Act, art. 9; art. 10 covers a lost or stolen card or login). From the moment the card company is told your debit card is lost or stolen, it pays for any use (Specialized Credit Financial Business Act, art. 16(1)). No law was found that limits what you lose before you tell it.

before: Specialized Credit Financial Business Act art. 16(2), with Enforcement Decree art. 6-9(1): the card company is liable for credit card use in the 60 days before it's told of loss or theft, and for everything after. Under art. 16(3) a written contract can shift part or all of that to a cardholder at fault. Under art. 16(5) the issuer bears forged cards, data stolen by hacking and cards issued in someone else's name, and under art. 16(10) it can't collect a disputed amount until it has investigated.
after: The card company pays for use of your credit card in the 60 days before it’s told of the loss or theft, and for everything after (Specialized Credit Financial Business Act, art. 16(2), and its Enforcement Decree, art. 6-9(1)). A written contract can pass some or all of that to you if you were at fault (art. 16(3)). The card company also bears forged cards, details stolen by hacking and cards issued in someone else’s name (art. 16(5)), and it can’t collect an amount you dispute until it has investigated (art. 16(10)).

before: No statutory refund deadline was found; art. 16(10) bars collecting a disputed credit card amount until the investigation ends.
after: No law was found that sets a deadline for a refund. A card company can’t collect a credit card amount you dispute until it has finished investigating (art. 16(10)).

before: ASIC's ePayments Code (June 2022), which covers ATM, EFTPOS, credit card, online and mobile payments: the holder isn't liable where it's clear they didn't contribute to the loss (cl. 10.3), or for fraud or negligence by bank staff, merchants or networks (cl. 10.1). Where a passcode was needed and fault can't be shown, liability is the least of $150, the balance available, or the loss before the report (cl. 11.7). If the bank proves the user contributed through fraud, a passcode breach or unreasonable delay, the holder bears actual losses before the report, within daily limits and the balance (cl. 11.2, 11.5).
after: You don’t pay where it’s clear you didn’t contribute to the loss (cl. 10.3), or for fraud or negligence by bank staff, shops or networks (cl. 10.1). Where a passcode was needed and no one can show who was at fault, you pay the least of A$150, the balance available, or what was lost before you reported it (cl. 11.7). If the bank proves you contributed through fraud, by not keeping your passcode secure or by reporting the loss unreasonably late, you pay what was actually lost before your report, within the daily limits and the balance (cl. 11.2, 11.5). This is ASIC’s ePayments Code (June 2022), which covers ATM, EFTPOS, credit card, online and mobile payments.

before: The ePayments Code covers credit card transactions, so the same rules apply: $0 if clearly not at fault, and a $150 limit where fault can't be shown (cl. 11.7). Clause 11.10 also requires the issuer to try card-scheme chargeback rights.
after: The ePayments Code covers credit card payments too, so the same rules apply: nothing if you clearly weren’t at fault, and at most A$150 where no one can show who was (cl. 11.7). The card issuer also has to try to get the money back through the card scheme’s chargeback rules (cl. 11.10).

before: ePayments Code cl. 18: within 21 days of a report the bank must finish investigating or explain in writing that it needs more time, and it must finish within 45 days unless circumstances are exceptional. The code sets no separate refund deadline.
after: Within 21 days of your report, the bank must finish investigating or tell you in writing that it needs more time, and it must finish within 45 days unless the circumstances are exceptional. The code sets no separate deadline for a refund (ePayments Code, cl. 18).

before: New Zealand Banking Association Code of Banking Practice (current edition, with scam commitments from November 30, 2025): the bank compensates losses from an unauthorized payment, meaning someone used your card or electronic banking without authority, if you weren't dishonest or negligent, took reasonable steps to protect your banking, and co-operate quickly. It's an industry code; no statute sets a dollar cap.
after: If someone uses your card or online banking without your permission, the bank pays you back, as long as you weren’t dishonest or negligent, took reasonable care to protect your banking, and cooperate with it quickly. This is the New Zealand Banking Association’s Code of Banking Practice (the current edition, with its scam commitments from November 30, 2025), an industry code: no law sets a dollar limit.

before: The Code of Banking Practice's unauthorized-payment promise covers cards generally, credit cards included: full compensation if you weren't dishonest or negligent. No statutory cap applies.
after: The Code of Banking Practice’s promise covers credit cards too: you’re paid back in full if you weren’t dishonest or negligent. No law sets a limit.

before: Code of Banking Practice: once the bank has the information it needs, it pays any compensation within 30 business days.
after: Once the bank has the information it needs, it pays you back within 30 business days (Code of Banking Practice).

before: Chase refuses to authorize any transaction once a card is reported lost or stolen, and sends a replacement card with a new number; for a credit card the account itself stays open and keeps its age for credit reporting.
after: Once you report a card lost or stolen, Chase declines anything new on it and sends a replacement with a new number. For a credit card, the account itself stays open and keeps its age on your credit record.

before: Chase monitors cards around the clock and may contact the customer by text message, push notification, email or phone call to confirm whether unusual activity was authorized; fraud alerts are automatic and need no enrollment. Chase can refuse to authorize a transaction it reasonably believes may be fraudulent, but doesn’t say it holds a payment pending the customer's reply.
after: Chase watches cards around the clock and may text, send an app notification, email or call to check that unusual activity was you. Fraud alerts are automatic: you don’t need to sign up. Chase can decline a payment it believes may be fraud, but it doesn’t say it holds a payment while it waits for your reply.

before: For a lost or stolen credit card, the bank says it will cancel the card and send a replacement right away. A debit card can be locked in Online Banking or the app while you look for it, and replaced there or by phone.
after: Bank of America says it cancels a lost or stolen credit card and sends a replacement right away. You can lock a debit card in Online Banking or the app while you look for it, and replace it there or by phone.

before: Wells Fargo’s rush is for credit cards: “We may be able to replace your card in as little as 24 hours (additional fees may apply)” (wellsfargo.com/help/lost-wallet), and its Active Cash card agreement names a Rush Plastic Fee without an amount.
after: Wells Fargo can rush a new credit card: “We may be able to replace your card in as little as 24 hours (additional fees may apply)” (wellsfargo.com/help/lost-wallet). Its Active Cash card agreement names a Rush Plastic Fee but gives no amount.

before: A lost or stolen debit or credit card is replaced with a new card number, expiration date and three-digit security code, arriving in about 5 to 7 calendar days. While you look for a misplaced card you can turn it off in the app or online, and recurring charges can still go through.
after: Wells Fargo replaces a lost or stolen debit or credit card with a new number, expiration date and security code, and it arrives in about 5 to 7 calendar days. While you look for a misplaced card, you can turn it off in the app or online, and recurring charges still go through.

before: If it sees unusual card activity, the bank may contact you by phone, email or text asking you to verify the transactions, and it may refuse to authorize a transaction it suspects is fraudulent. Its texts come from short codes such as 93557.
after: If Wells Fargo sees unusual card activity, it may call, email or text to ask whether the payments were you, and it may decline a payment it suspects is fraud. Its texts come from short codes such as 93557.

before: A replaced credit card comes with a different number, security code and expiration date, usually within about 5 business days. Citi Quick Lock in the app or online blocks new charges on a misplaced card while letting recurring charges continue.
after: A replacement credit card has a new number, security code and expiration date, and usually arrives within about 5 business days. Citi Quick Lock, in the app or online, blocks new charges on a misplaced card and lets recurring charges continue.

before: When a credit card is reported lost or stolen, Capital One locks it and issues a replacement with a new card number, arriving in about 4 to 6 business days; a lost debit card is deactivated immediately. Eligible customers can use a virtual card in the app while they wait.
after: When you report a credit card lost or stolen, Capital One locks it and sends a replacement with a new number in about 4 to 6 business days. A lost debit card is turned off at once. If you’re eligible, you can use a virtual card in the app while you wait.

before: If Capital One sees possibly suspicious activity it sends a text, always from the same number, and you can reply on the spot; answering no blocks the card. Alerts also come by email and in the app.
after: If Capital One sees activity that might be fraud, it texts you, always from the same number, and you can reply on the spot. Answering no blocks the card. Alerts also come by email and in the app.

before: RBC cancels a lost or stolen debit card and issues a new one, and blocks a lost or stolen credit card from further use and issues a new card. The first debit card replacement in a calendar year is free and each further one costs $5.00, unless the replacement is due to fraud, a name change, or a card that arrived damaged.
after: RBC cancels a lost or stolen debit card and sends a new one, and blocks a lost or stolen credit card and sends a new card. Your first replacement debit card in a calendar year is free, and each one after that costs C$5.00, unless it’s replaced because of fraud, a name change or a card that arrived damaged. The game charges nothing for any of them.

before: RBC texts the credit cardholder from short code 722373 or 347722 asking them to reply Y to confirm a transaction or N if they don't recognize it, after which a fraud specialist contacts them. The card agreement says RBC can block the card without telling the customer when it suspects fraudulent use.
after: On a credit card, RBC texts you from short code 722373 or 347722. Reply Y to confirm a payment, or N if you don’t recognize it, and a fraud specialist contacts you. The card agreement says RBC can block the card without telling you when it suspects fraud.

before: TD closes a lost, stolen or compromised Access Card permanently and issues a replacement that arrives by Canada Post in 5 to 7 business days, or can be picked up the same day at a branch. The customer can lock the card instantly in the TD app while looking for it.
after: TD closes a lost, stolen or compromised Access Card for good and sends a replacement by Canada Post in 5 to 7 business days, or you can pick one up the same day at a branch. You can lock the card instantly in the TD app while you look for it.

before: TD texts the credit cardholder when it detects suspicious activity and blocks the card; replying Y unblocks it immediately, while replying N or not answering keeps it blocked until the customer calls, and TD phones if there’s no reply. TD's published fraud alerts cover credit cards; the page doesn’t mention debit cards.
after: When TD sees suspicious activity on a credit card, it blocks the card and texts you. Reply Y and it’s unblocked at once. Reply N, or don’t answer, and it stays blocked until you call; TD phones you if you don’t reply. TD’s fraud alerts page covers credit cards and doesn’t mention debit cards.

before: A lost or stolen ScotiaCard debit card is reported and replaced in the Scotia app, with the new card arriving in 5 to 10 business days; a lost credit card is reported by phone and the replacement arrives in about 7 to 10 business days. A locked debit card still lets pre-authorized payments and bills set up on it go through.
after: You report a lost or stolen ScotiaCard debit card in the Scotia app and order its replacement there, and the new card arrives in 5 to 10 business days.
